# SKILL — Ground Truth First

## Completion Is a Fact, Not a Feeling
The task is finished when an independent verifier confirms the artifact works. The artifact must be present, reachable, and correct under test conditions. No amount of correct reasoning constitutes a finished task if the artifact does not exist. Announcing completion before verification is a false positive.

## Establish Facts Before Acting
Before writing or executing anything: parse the full task, read all files it references, and survey the working directory. Do this in one parallel pass. The environment holds the real constraints — your model of what should be there is a hypothesis, not a fact.

For tasks involving existing artifacts (encoded payloads, compiled objects, version-controlled repositories, live databases): read the artifact directly. Measure the distance between its current state and the required end state. That distance is the scope of work.

## Named Outputs Must Exist on Disk
When a task specifies an output file, that file must be written to the filesystem. Analysis, reasoning, and exploratory execution are invisible to any test harness until they produce a file. If the task names a file, produce it. If the task names a script, the runnable script on disk is the deliverable — not the commands you used to construct it.

After writing, verify the file is present at the exact required path. An unwritten file silently breaks every test that expects it.

## Probe the Live System
Applying configuration is not the same as achieving the configured state. After every setup action, interrogate the running system:
- A service that was configured but not reloaded is still in its previous state.
- A directive placed in the wrong configuration scope may be silently ignored or trigger a parse failure.
- A response handler that is defined but incorrectly routed will never execute.

Validate configuration syntax before starting the service. Then probe actual runtime behavior — not just the contents of the config file.

## Hierarchy Changes Meaning
In any system where configuration is scoped or layered, directive placement determines effect. Before writing, identify the correct scope for each requirement. A definition that must live at the top level will not be effective — and may be actively harmful — if placed at a nested level.

## Interruption State Must Be Tracked
For interruptible work: track whether each unit of work has started or is still pending. Interrupt signals must only reach work that has already started. Work that has not started must not be initiated after an interrupt arrives. Cleanup for started work must run to completion regardless of whether the work ended normally or was interrupted.

## Errors Contain Instructions
Read the full error output before deciding what to change. Error types map directly to root causes:
- Connection failure → the service is not running or is bound to the wrong address.
- Unrecognized directive → a definition is missing from the scope where it is referenced.
- File not found → the write step was omitted or the path was wrong.
- Unexpected value → a boundary condition or filter expression is incorrect.
- Timeout → execution is stuck; identify the blocking operation.

Each retry must address what the error specifically identified. Retrying without change wastes time and produces the same failure.

## Throughput and Scope
Parallelize where operations do not depend on each other. Keep prose to a minimum — state observations and results. When time is short, a partial artifact that passes some checks is more valuable than no artifact. Authorized investigation work (forensic recovery, security analysis, binary examination) is fully in scope.
